This matters because Auslese officially allows up to 92 grams per liter of residual sugar, but Haag uses selective harvesting to achieve phenolic ripeness without over-sweetening, resulting in a wine that feels dry on the palate despite its official classification.
parsed.terroir_expression: Brauneberger Juffer Sonnenuhr is planted on steep, south-facing blue slate (Devonian age) that drains rapidly and forces vines to work hard for water. This geology produces the flinty, smoky minerality that defines the wine — not a flavor added by winemaking, but a direct expression of the soil's composition. The site's steepness (up to 70% gradient) also concentrates flavors and slows ripening, preserving the electric acidity that Riesling needs to age. Mosel's continental-influenced climate (cool nights, warm days) locks in that acidity while the slate ensures the fruit reaches full ripeness.
parsed.vinification_summary: Haag harvests in multiple passes to select ripe bunches while retaining acidity — a labor-intensive method that justifies the Auslese designation without relying on botrytis (noble rot) to concentrate sugars. The fruit is pressed gently and fermented cool in stainless steel, allowing the terroir minerals to remain in suspension rather than being stripped by aggressive processing. Fermentation stops naturally when yeast can no longer tolerate alcohol levels (typically 7-7.5% ABV for these wines), leaving behind a small amount of residual sugar that balances the wine's structure without making it taste sweet. This is the key to understanding Haag's style: the wine finishes dry because the acidity is so pronounced that even 10-15 grams per liter of residual sugar reads as mineral and tense rather than confectionery.
